How Car Accidents Cause Hearing Loss

Car accidents can damage your hearing in several ways that some accident victims do not initially consider. Discovering how victims may damage their hearing during a car crash could help you gain more knowledge on the type of injuries that you have and how they may become severe.

Loud Noises and Trauma

The explosive sound of a collision can exceed 140 decibels, which is louder than a jet engine at takeoff. This intense noise can immediately damage the delicate hair cells in your inner ear that transmit sound signals to your brain. Even exposure to these extreme sound levels can cause permanent hearing damage or tinnitus (persistent ringing in the ears).

Airbag Deployment

Modern vehicles' lifesaving airbags deploy at speeds exceeding 200 mph, creating a shockwave and explosion that reaches 160 to 175 decibels. This sudden pressure change occurs inches from your ears, potentially causing:
  • Rupture of the eardrum (tympanic membrane)
  • Damage to the ossicles (tiny bones that transmit sound)
  • Acoustic trauma to inner ear structures

Head Trauma and TBI

The violent forces in a collision often cause your head to strike objects or the interior of the vehicle. These impacts can result in:
  • Temporal bone fractures affecting the ear canal
  • Labyrinthine concussion disrupting inner ear fluid
  • Traumatic brain injury affecting how your brain processes sound
  • Damage to auditory nerves carrying signals from ear to brain

Blood Flow Disruption

Neck injuries are common in car accidents and could temporarily or permanently alter blood flow to the inner ear, causing oxygen deprivation. Even brief interruptions to this blood supply can result in sudden loss of hearing.

Secondary Infections and Inflammation

Trauma to the ear region can create pathways for infection or trigger inflammatory responses that cause delayed hearing loss days or weeks after your accident. This delayed onset often leads victims to overlook the connection to their crash. Accident-related hearing damage often appears immediately but can also develop gradually in the days and weeks following your crash. This is why prompt medical evaluation is crucial after any collision, even if you initially feel fine.

What Type of Hearing Problems Victims Have After a Car Accident?

Due to the impact and forces involved in a car accident, victims are vulnerable to various types of injuries. Some of the injuries victims might experience could be:
  • Muffled Hearing: This may feel like listening underwater or having cotton in your ears. It can be caused by ear trauma, whiplash or a burst eardrum.
  • Tinnitus: Ringing, buzzing or hissing sounds in the ears, often following head or neck injuries.
  • Hearing Loss: This can be either temporary or permanent and is often caused by damage to the inner ear structures or auditory pathways.
  • Dizziness or Vertigo: These symptoms can indicate inner ear damage, affecting balance and hearing.
  • Ear Pain or Fullness: A sensation of pressure or fullness in the ears, which might suggest damage affecting hearing acuity
  • Conductive Hearing Loss: This occurs when sound waves cannot travel efficiently through the outer ear, ear canal, or middle ear to reach the inner ear.
  • Sensorineural Hearing Loss: SHL is caused by damage to the inner ear or the auditory nerve pathways. This typically occurs after loud noises or infections.
  • Mixed Hearing Loss: A combination of conductive and sensorineural hearing loss. This means there are issues in the outer or middle ear, the inner ear, or the auditory nerve.
  • Hyperacusis: A rare condition where sounds are perceived as unbearably loud and painful daily.

  • Consistent Medical Treatment: Maintain follow-up appointments and comply with recommended treatment to show the validity of your condition. It also creates an ongoing record of your hearing issues and their impact on your life.
  • Daily Impact Documentation: Keep a detailed journal describing how your hearing loss affects your daily activities, work performance, relationships and emotional well-being. This step can help quantify non-economic damages and reinforce the seriousness of your injuries.

Top Reasons Why Claims May Get Unfairly Denied

Insurance companies scrutinize every car accident claim that comes their way. Even when you believe your case is straightforward, insurers have numerous tactics to justify denial. Below are common reasons for claim denials. Knowing the reasons can help you avoid potential pitfalls.

Disputes About Fault and Liability

South Carolina follows "comparative negligence" rules, meaning your compensation decrease is based on your percentage of fault. You may receive nothing if they can prove you were 51 percent or more responsible. Insurance companies frequently challenge who was responsible for the accident by:
  • Claiming you were partially or fully at fault
  • Arguing that a third party caused the accident
  • Disputing police report findings
  • Questioning witness credibility
  • Using unclear traffic laws to shift blame

The Pre-existing Condition Defense

Insurance companies may say that your conditions are related to pre-existing conditions that you had before the accident. They may argue that your injuries are not related to the accident. This tactic is particularly effective because many injuries, especially neck and back problems, can have symptoms similar to pre-existing conditions. Common denial tactics that may involve your pre-existing medical history are:
  • Claiming your injuries existed before the accident
  • Attributing your pain to age-related degeneration rather than the crash
  • Suggesting your current treatment relates to previous injuries
  • Requesting extensive past medical records to find any similar complaints
  • Arguing that you failed to disclose relevant medical history

Minimizing Your Injury Severity

Some insurance companies may hire medical professionals to review your records without examining you personally, allowing them to dispute your doctor's observations. Insurance companies routinely downplay how serious your injuries are by:
  • Questioning why you did not seek immediate medical attention
  • Suggesting your treatment was excessive for your injuries
  • Claiming specific treatments were not medically necessary
  • Using their medical examiners who typically minimize injuries
  • Arguing that your pain and suffering claims are exaggerated

Inconsistencies in Your Statements

Insurance adjusters are trained to look for inconsistencies, often asking the same questions in different ways to catch you in a contradiction. Any of the following discrepancies of the accident can lead to denial:
  • Contradictions between your initial report and later statements
  • Differences between what you tell doctors versus what you tell insurance adjusters
  • Inconsistencies between your account and the police report
  • Social media posts that contradict your claimed injuries
  • Surveillance evidence that does not match your disability claims

Sneaky Insurance Company Tactics to Watch For

Insurance companies have refined their claims-handling strategies over decades, developing sophisticated methods to minimize payouts. After a Charleston car accident, be alert for these deceptive tactics that could significantly impact your compensation.
  • Quick Settlement Trap: Insurance companies may offer you a settlement within days or hours after your car accident without you knowing the extent of your injuries.
  • Recorded Statements: Insurance companies may try to minimize your claim by recording and asking you misleading questions about fault or injuries.
  • Delays to Wear You Down: Insurers may stretch out the claims process, hoping you will become desperate enough to accept lowball offers due to mounting medical bills or missing work.
  • Surveillance and Social Media Monitoring: Insurers may hire private investigators to document you engaging in physical activities to prove that you are exaggerating your limitations.
  • Medical Record Manipulation: Insurers may request excessive medical history to find pre-existing conditions and could take physicians' notes out of context.
  • Misrepresenting Your Coverage Rights: Most adjusters mistakenly tell you that certain damages are not covered because they may think you are unfamiliar with insurance policies and South Carolina law.

South Carolina Insurance Laws That Protect You

South Carolina operates under a fault-based system. This means the insurance of the at-fault driver is primarily responsible for covering damages. In South Carolina, insurers are required to offer uninsured motorist coverage equal to your liability limits. This protection covers you when a driver hits you without insurance. If you are a hit-and-run victim or an at-fault driver’s insurance company cannot pay your claims, uninsured motorist coverage can cover you. Bad faith insurance laws protect South Carolina’s accident victims. These laws prevent insurers from denying valid claims without facing consequences. Some examples of bad faith practices include refusing proper investigations, denying claims without reasonable justification and offering settlements far below obvious claim value.

What Evidence Protects Your Right to Compensation

Strong evidence can help victims get the compensation they need to recover after a car accident. Critical Evidence at the Accident Scene

Police Report Documentation

Witness Statements and Contact Information

Medical Documentation

Digital and Electronic Evidence

Testimony and Reports

What Is Brake Checking?

Brake-checking is a dangerous driving behavior where a driver deliberately and suddenly applies their brakes when another vehicle is following closely behind. This action forces the following driver to brake abruptly or take risky actions to avoid a collision.

Why Drivers Brake Check and How It Endangers Motorists

Drivers may brake-check on highways when they feel someone is tailgating them. During road rage or aggression, drivers may feel pumped up to teach another driver a lesson, who they think is driving improperly. In high-traffic situations, drivers could get frustrated by another’s actions, especially if vehicles move slowly. Brake-checking can endanger drivers' safety because they can be in a hazardous car accident. In some cases, drivers can get involved in an altercation if brake-checking results from road rage.

How South Carolina’s 51 Percent Fault Rule Affects Brake-Checking Accidents

South Carolina operates on a modified comparative negligence law. This means you can still recover damages from a car crash as long as you are less than 50 percent at fault. The percentage of fault assessed against you directly determines your eligibility to recover compensation. Even a one percent difference can mean the difference between a partial recovery and no recovery at all. If you are 51 percent or greater at fault, you will not be able to recover compensation.

Types of Evidence That Can Prove Brake Checking in Charleston

If you were injured in a brake-checking crash, you will need compelling evidence to overcome the typical presumption that the tailing driver is always at fault for a rear-end crash. The most effective types of evidence that can establish a brake-checking claim includes:

Dashcam and Traffic Camera Footage

Video evidence provides the most definitive proof of brake checking. Dashcam footage showing a vehicle suddenly braking without apparent reason is powerful evidence in Charleston courts. Look for:
  • Clear views of the lead vehicle's brake lights activating suddenly
  • Absence of traffic or road hazards that would justify braking
  • Multiple braking episodes suggesting intentional behavior
  • The lead driver's actions before the brake-checking incident

Witness Testimony

Witnesses can provide testimony about a brake-checking incident. Charleston's busy roads often mean multiple drivers observe these dangerous maneuvers. Compelling witness testimony typically includes:
  • Observations of aggressive driving before the incident
  • Confirmation that no road hazards existed to justify sudden braking
  • Descriptions of multiple brake-checking attempts
  • Statements about the lead driver's behavior suggesting road rage

Electronic Vehicle Data

Various types of electronic data from the vehicles involved may provide additional evidence that support brake-checking claims in Charleston courts. Modern vehicles record extensive data that can be extracted after accidents:
  • Event Data Recorders (EDRs) capture sudden changes in speed, such as if the driver had to slam on the brakes
  • Braking patterns may show unusual or unnecessary braking
  • Speed data may reveal inconsistent driving behavior

Physical Evidence and Accident Reconstruction

An accident reconstructionist uses physical evidence from the scene, along with high tech tools to establish what happened. This type of evidence may include:
  • Skid mark patterns in the road, which indicates the driver had to brake suddenly
  • Impact analysis revealing the position and speeds of both vehicles
  • Damage patterns to involved vehicles that are consistent with sudden, unexpected braking
  • Road conditions that do not justify emergency stops

Steps to Take Immediately if You Are a Victim of Brake Checking

When another driver brake-checks you, act quickly to protect your safety and strengthen your legal claim. Pull over to a safe location if possible. After a collision, turn on your hazard lights and move to the shoulder or a nearby parking area, provided your vehicle is drivable. Stay in your car if getting out would endanger you, especially on highways and busy roads.

Call Law Enforcement

After a brake-checking car accident, call law enforcement to report the accident. When officers arrive, explain what happened without involving your emotions. Statements like “This driver made me mad” or “I am so annoyed” could be documented in a police report as a part of a police officer’s observation. A police officer can say you were upset or angry, which could misinterpret what happened during a car crash. Calmly describe the driver’s behavior before and during the brake check accident and remember to ask for a copy of the police report.

Document the Accident Scene

Document everything at the scene of the accident. Gather as much evidence as possible by taking photos of vehicles and license plates. Pictures of road conditions and weather can showcase what occurs during an accident.

Notify Your Insurance Company

Call your insurance company to inform them about the accident. Stick to essential information such as the accident's date, time and location. Avoid discussing fault until you have consulted with an attorney.

What Kinds of Facial Injuries Happen in Car Crashes?

A car accident can cause serious damage to facial bones, muscles, nerves and soft tissues. Below are some of the most common types of facial injuries caused by car crashes.

Soft Tissue Injuries

Cuts, bruises and burns across the face can result from broken glass or flying debris during a car accident. These injuries may range from minor scrapes to deep lacerations requiring plastic surgery. Even seemingly minor cuts on the face can leave permanent scars, affecting a victim's appearance and emotional well-being.

Facial Fractures

The face contains 14 different bones that can break during trauma. Common fractures include orbital fractures, which affect the eye socket, and cheekbone fractures, which are more likely to happen in side-impact collisions. Other types of fractures may include:
  • Nasal bone breaks from direct impacts
  • Cheekbone (zygomatic) fractures from side impacts
  • Jaw (mandible) fractures that affect eating and speaking
  • Upper jaw (maxilla) fractures requiring surgical repair

Dental Trauma

Dental trauma in a car accident typically happens when your head or mouth strikes an object or when the mouth abruptly closes due to the impact. For example, in a rear-end car accident, someone’s head or mouth can strike the steering wheel. Dental injuries during a car accident could be:
  • Broken or chipped teeth
  • Knocked-out teeth requiring immediate care
  • Fractured dental roots
  • Damaged gums and soft tissue
  • Jaw alignment problems affecting the victim's bite

Eye Injuries Trauma

Eye injuries from a car crash could leave victims with blurry vision or vision loss. Eye injuries may occur if the victim is struck in the face with a direct impact, such as from airbag deployment or shattered glass. Serious eye injuries may include:
  • Corneal scratches or tears
  • Orbital bone damage
  • Vision problems
  • Detached retina
  • Loss of eyesight

Nerve Damage

Facial injuries often involve some degree of nerve damage. The impact of a trauma may stretch, compress or even sever nerves. In a car accident, facial nerve damage happens when the impact forces the head or face against hard surfaces. Nerve damage may cause car crash victims to experience:
  • Loss of facial movement
  • Numbness or tingling
  • Problems with facial expressions
  • Difficulty eating or speaking
  • Chronic pain

Common Causes of Facial Scarring and Disfigurement

During a car crash, multiple factors can lead to facial scarring and disfigurement. The impact of a collision can be severe enough to thrust a victim's body and face against hard surfaces in the vehicle. Facial scarring and disfigurement may occur in a car crash as a result of:

Flying Glass and Debris

Shattered windshields and windows send sharp glass fragments flying through the vehicle at high speeds. These fragments can slice deep into facial tissue, causing severe lacerations that often result in permanent scarring. Side-impact collisions particularly increase the risk of glass-related facial injuries when windows explode inward.

Airbag Deployment Impact

While airbags save lives, their explosive deployment can cause serious facial injuries. The intense force and heat from deploying airbags can burn the skin, cause chemical burns or create facial abrasions. High-speed deployment may also drive debris into facial tissue.

Dashboard and Steering Wheel Impact

Sudden deceleration can throw drivers and passengers forward onto hard surfaces, like the dashboard or steering wheel. The resulting impact can break or crush facial bones and create wounds that cause permanent disfigurement.

Ejection Injuries

When victims get thrown from vehicles, their faces may hit window glass, metal from the vehicle or scrape across pavement. Road rash from sliding across asphalt can remove layers of facial skin. Additionally, impact with objects during ejection can shatter facial bones and create deep tissue damage.

Secondary Collision Damage

After the initial impact, loose objects inside the car become dangerous projectiles. Cell phones, water bottles and other items could strike the face. These secondary impacts often cause significant tissue damage and scarring.

Metal and Frame Intrusion

Sharp metal edges can penetrate the passenger compartment when a vehicle's frame collapses during impact. These twisted metal pieces can slice or puncture facial tissue, creating jagged wounds that are difficult to repair without visible scarring.

Burns and Chemical Exposure

Vehicle fires or chemical spills during crashes can cause severe facial burns. Thermal burns destroy tissue layers, while chemical burns from deployed airbags or leaking fluids can create permanent skin damage and discoloration.

Reasons Drivers Act Recklessly

Drivers engage in reckless behavior for psychological and situational reasons. Emotional states like rage, frustration or aggression often trigger dangerous driving choices. Some drivers feel invincible behind the wheel, causing them to speed, tailgate or weave through traffic without considering the consequences. Young or inexperienced drivers may lack proper risk assessment skills or feel peer pressure to drive dangerously. Some drivers disregard traffic laws, viewing them as inconvenient rather than essential safety measures. This combination of personal, emotional and situational factors creates dangerous conditions on heavily trafficked Charleston roads like I-26. Time pressure plays a significant role. Some drivers may be running late, causing them to rush to work or appointments, resulting in unnecessary risks. Other interruptions can lead to reckless drivers. Distraction from phones, passengers or other activities diverts attention from safe driving practices. Substances like alcohol and drugs can severely impair judgment and reaction time. If drivers take prescription drugs before they drive, it can also alter their behavior and become the root cause of their reckless driving.

What Are the Most Common Forms of Reckless Driving?

Reckless drivers have various types of behaviors and activities that they do. Some of the most common forms of reckless driving are:
  • Distracted Driving: This includes activities like texting, eating, adjusting your seat or review mirror while driving.
  • Speeding: Driving above the speed limit reduces reaction time and increases the risk of accidents.
  • Aggressive Driving: This involves tailgating, weaving through traffic or not yielding to other vehicles
  • Street Racing: Racing on public roads is hazardous and illegal
  • Disregarding Traffic Signs and Laws: Running red lights or not stopping at stop signs

How Does Reckless Driving Lead to an Accident?

Reckless driving creates dangerous situations that quickly escalate into crashes. Excessive speed reduces reaction time and increases impact force. When drivers weave through traffic or tailgate, they leave no safety margin for sudden stops or emergencies. Weather conditions and the flow of traffic could amplify these risks. During coastal storms or heavy tourism seasons, reckless driving becomes especially dangerous on routes like Highway 17 and the Ravenel Bridge. Roads already crowded with commuters, tourists and port traffic become hazardous when reckless drivers ignore safety protocols. In some incidents, reckless drivers can cause multiple-vehicle car accidents. Erratically changing lanes or running a red light can cause multiple vehicle accidents. These chain-reaction accidents frequently cause severe injuries and extensive property damage.

Are Reckless Drivers Always Liable for An Accident?

Reckless drivers typically bear primary liability for accidents, but other factors can influence fault. These drivers must generally prove another party's negligence contributed to the crash to reduce their liability. Contributing factors that may affect liability:
  • Road conditions or maintenance issues
  • Vehicle mechanical failures
  • Other drivers' reactions
  • Traffic signal malfunctions
In some cases, both parties may share fault for the car accident. This is called a modified comparative negligence system. In South Carolina, if both parties are found to be partially at fault, each party’s compensation will be reduced by their percentage of fault. For example, if you are found to be 30 percent at fault for an accident and your total settlement amount is $100,000, you will only receive $70,000. Note that a party cannot recover compensation if they are more than 50 percent at fault.

What Should I Do If I Encounter a Reckless Driver on The Road?

If you encounter a reckless driver, prioritize your safety by creating distance between your vehicle and theirs. Never engage with or challenge aggressive drivers. Key actions to take:
  • Pull over safely or change lanes to let them pass
  • Maintain a safe following distance
  • Call 911 to report dangerous driving
  • Note the vehicle description and license plate if safe
  • Exit the highway or take an alternate route if needed

What Is a Traumatic Brain Injury?

A Traumatic Brain Injury (TBI) occurs when a sudden trauma causes damage to the brain. This damage can result from the head violently hitting an object, an object piercing the skull and entering brain tissue or forces that cause the brain to move within the skull, such as violent shaking or blast waves.

How Do Car Crashes Cause Serious Brain Injuries?

Car crashes can cause severe brain injuries through several types of incidents that happen during a car crash. Some incidents may include:
  • Direct Impact Trauma: When the head strikes objects like the steering wheel, windshield, or side window, the force can fracture the skull and damage brain tissue directly.
  • Acceleration-Deceleration Forces: Even without direct head impact, rapid acceleration and deceleration causes the brain to collide with the inner skull wall. This creates bruising (contusions) and tearing of nerve fibers (diffuse axonal injury).
  • Penetrating Injuries: Broken glass, metal fragments or other debris can pierce the skull and enter brain tissue.

Car Crashes Factors Affecting Severity of Injuries

The severity of injuries depends on factors like the vehicle speed at impact and the direction of the collision. If a car crash victim did not wear a seat belt, it could increase the severity of their injuries. In some cases, passengers sitting in the front of the vehicle are more likely to suffer from more serious injuries. Older cars with fewer safety features than newer cars could have higher impacts, which may result in more severe injuries.

Secondary Injuries Worsening Health Conditions

Secondary injuries often develop after the initial trauma due to brain swelling or internal bleeding. These injuries frequently affect vital brain regions that control movement, cognition, speech and other vital functions. Prompt medical treatment is essential to prevent worsening damage and improve recovery outcomes.

What Types of Traumatic Brain Injuries Are Common in Car Crashes?

The violent forces involved in collisions can damage the brain in various ways, from mild concussions to severe trauma requiring intensive medical intervention. Victims should know the different types of brain injuries that can happen in a car crash to help with their recovery, a potential legal case and to navigate through life-altering conditions.

Concussions

A concussion is a type of traumatic brain injury that is caused when your brain collides with the inside of your skull. During a car crash, the sudden stop or impact forces cause your brain to bounce or twist inside the skull. Some of the key symptoms of a concussion:
  • Headaches
  • Confusion
  • Memory problems
  • Vision changes
  • Balance issues
  • Nausea
  • Sensitivity to light/noise
  • Sleep disturbances

Hematomas and Hemorrhages

A violent car crash can tear blood vessels in your brain, leading to two types of life-threatening conditions. One is a hematoma, which occurs when blood collects between your brain and skull, creating dangerous pressure on delicate brain tissue. These blood pools may develop slowly over hours or days after the accident, making them particularly dangerous. Brain hemorrhages present a greater threat, as active bleeding within the brain tissue itself can cause rapid deterioration. The bleeding damages surrounding brain cells and creates swelling that can lead to permanent injury or death without immediate treatment. After any head impact, watch out for severe headaches that intensify, growing confusion, slurred speech and seizures.

Brain Contusions

A brain contusion is bruising of brain tissue that occurs when the force of a crash causes your brain to hit your skull. Like bruises elsewhere on your body, these injuries involve bleeding and swelling inside your brain, which can be life-threatening. Some car crash victims may experience confusion and coordination problems.

Skull Fracture

A skull fracture may occur if a violent car crash impact causes you to crack or shatter your skull. These breaks range from hairline cracks to deep fractures that expose brain tissue.

Coup-Contrecoup Injury

A coup-contrecoup injury is a serious type of traumatic brain injury (TBI) that involves damage at two sites in the brain. The coup is at the site of direct impact, while the opposite side of the brain is known as contrecoup. Symptoms vary depending on which areas of the brain are affected, but may include loss of consciousness, memory problems, nausea and vomiting.

Diffuse Axonal Injury

Car crash victims may sustain diffuse axonal injuries after sudden movement stretches and tears axons, nerve fibers, throughout the brain’s white matter.

Why Do Insurance Companies Fight Brain Injury Claims?

Insurance companies often challenge brain injury claims using tactics to help minimize payouts and protect company profits. Their goals do not align with yours, so they make low initial settlement offers to protect their interests. Other tactics they may try include delaying claim processing or extensively perusing victims' medical histories and social media in an attempt to find contradicting evidence. They frequently dispute causation, arguing symptoms existed before the accident or stem from other conditions. They may even question the severity of your brain injury, especially with mild TBIs where damage may not be visible on standard imaging tests. Insurance companies know brain injury claims can be expensive, potentially involving lifetime care costs, lost wages and reduced earning capacity. They also recognize that proving non-obvious symptoms like cognitive difficulties or personality changes can be challenging for victims. Therefore, it is vital to have solid evidence that links your injuries to the car accident.

What Medical Evidence Can Help to Support My Brain Injury Claim?

Strong medical evidence for brain injury claims includes:
  • Medical Records: Documents from the emergency room and hospital visits, treating physician notes, assessments and neurologist evaluations.
  • Diagnostic Tests: CT, MRI and PET scans can detect what type of TBI car crash victims have, along with EEGs.
  • Specialist Documentation: If car crash victims visit a specialist for their injuries, they can provide neuropsychological evaluations, cognitive function test results and speech or occupational therapy assessments.
  • Supporting Evidence: This type of evidence may include photos of visible injuries, witness statements about behavioral changes and work or school performance records showing decline.

What Should You Tell Your Health Provider About Your Injuries?

Explain How the Injury Happened

Previous Injuries

All Your Symptoms

Report every symptom you experience, even those that seem minor or unrelated. Seemingly minor symptoms may indicate more serious underlying injuries. Be sure to share symptoms such as sleep disturbances, headaches, or dizziness with your healthcare provider. Keep a pain journal to document your pain levels. Include any memory or concentration issues, changes in mobility and emotional changes like anxiety or depression. Thorough documentation can provide valuable information for both your medical treatment and any potential legal claims.

The Impact Injuries Have on Your Daily Life

For instance, if your injuries impact your ability to play with your children or help them with their homework, be sure to inform your doctor. Injuries that impact your social and work life can tie into compensation for loss wages or emotional distress.

Questions

What Is the Most Common Shoulder Injury From a Car Accident?

Car accidents frequently cause various shoulder injuries, with rotator cuff tears being the most common. The rotator cuff consists of four muscles and tendons that stabilize your shoulder joint and enable arm movement. During a collision, the sudden impact can cause these tissues to stretch, tear or become severely damaged. While rotator cuff injuries are one of the most frequent injuries, other common shoulder injuries from car accidents include:
  • Shoulder Fractures: Breaks in the bones of the shoulder can cause victims to experience severe pain, swelling and difficulty moving the arm.
  • Shoulder Dislocation: This occurs when the upper arm bone pops out of the shoulder socket, causing intense pain and limited mobility.
  • Labral Tears: The labrum is a ring of cartilage that surrounds the shoulder socket and helps keep the joint stable. Tears in this cartilage can lead to pain and instability in the shoulder.
  • Bursitis: This involves inflammation of small, fluid-filled sacs that cushion your joints and reduce friction between bones, tendons and muscles. This may lead to pain and swelling, particularly during arm movement.
  • AC Joint Separation: This may happen when the joint connecting your collarbone to shoulder blade becomes damaged due to a fall or direct blow to the shoulder, leading to a visible bump on the shoulder.
Shoulder injuries occur when the body is thrown forward during impact, especially if you are gripping the steering wheel tightly. Side-impact collisions can also cause direct trauma to the shoulder area.

How Do I Know if My Shoulder Injuries Are Severe?

Recognizing the severity of a shoulder injury early can ensure you receive proper treatment and detailed documentation for your injury claim. Warning signs of a serious shoulder injury include:
  • Visible deformity or swelling

  • Inability to raise your arm above your head
  • Inability to raise your arm above your head
  • Pain that worsens at night or prevents sleep
  • Numbness or tingling extending down your arm
  • A popping or grinding sensation when moving your shoulder
Do not dismiss these symptoms as minor or temporary. Some shoulder injuries may seem manageable initially but can become worse without proper medical attention. Additionally, adrenaline released during the accident can mask pain, making injuries appear less severe than they are.

Do I Have the Right To Refuse Certain Medical Treatment?

Yes, you absolutely have the legal right to refuse medical treatment after a car accident. This right is protected under both state and federal law, stemming from the fundamental principle of bodily autonomy. However, understanding the consequences of this decision is essential. Medical professionals recommend treatment to ensure your well-being and document any injuries diagnosed as a result of a car accident. Even if you do not think you have any injuries seek medical attention. Some injuries may not be apparent right away. Injuries like whiplash or internal bleeding can have delayed symptoms that worsen over time. When you refuse medical treatment, you might be putting both your health and your legal right at risk.

How Can Refusing Medical Treatment Impact My Claim?

The decision to refuse medical treatment can have profound consequences for your car accident claim. Insurance companies and defense attorneys will scrutinize every aspect of your case, including your medical decisions.

Weakens Your Injury Claim Evidence

Medical documentation serves as crucial evidence in personal injury cases. When you seek immediate medical attention, healthcare providers create detailed records that gives insight into your injuries, treatment plans and prognosis. These records establish a clear link between the accident and your injuries, strengthening your claim. Without this documentation, proving the extent and cause of your injuries becomes significantly more challenging.

No Evidence for Pain and Suffering

Medical records provide objective evidence of your pain and suffering. For example, they can give insight into why you have chronic pain and how difficult your physical therapy appointments are. When you refuse treatment, you lose the opportunity to have professional documentation of your condition immediately after the accident, which can be difficult to reconstruct later.

Gives Insurers Reason To Deny Payment

Insurance companies are always looking for reasons to minimize or deny claims. Refusing medical treatment gives them powerful ammunition to argue that your injuries were not serious or were not caused by the accident. They might insist that if you were truly injured, you would have sought immediate medical attention. Insurance adjusters may also argue that your injuries worsened because you did not seek prompt medical care, making you partially responsible for your current condition. Their assumptions could lead to claims denial.

Decrease the Value of Your Claim

When calculating the value of your claim, insurance companies and courts look at various factors, including the promptness and consistency of your medical treatment. Refusing treatment can significantly decrease your claim's value because:
  • The gap between the accident and your eventual treatment makes it harder to prove causation
  • Your injuries may have worsened, but the insurer can argue this was due to your negligence in seeking treatment
  • The lack of immediate medical documentation makes it difficult to establish the initial severity of your injuries

What Evidence Should I Gather if I Refuse Medical Treatment After a Car Crash?

If you refuse medical treatment after a car crash, it can be more challenging to prove your injuries and claim compensation. However, you can still gather other evidence to support your case, such as:
  • Police Report: This document provides an official account of the incident and can help establish fault.
  • Photographs and Videos: Visual evidence can help demonstrate the severity of the crash.
  • Witness Statements: Witnesses account of what happened at the car crash scene can align with your version of events, which can help strengthen your case.
  • Receipts and Bills: Save all your receipts related to expenses incurred due to the accident, like vehicle repairs, transportation costs, and any over-the-counter medications or treatment you purchased.
  • Employment Records: Document any time missed from work and any impact on your ability to perform your job. This could show the financial impact the accident had on your injuries.

Reasons Car Crash Victims Refuse Treatment

Car crash victims may refuse medical treatment for several reasons. Sometimes victims may refuse treatment if they have a suspicion or a concern that they think may hinder them. Common reasons include:
  • Fear of missing work or losing income
  • Anxiety about medical procedures or hospitals
  • Belief that injuries are minor and will heal on their own
  • Religious or personal beliefs about certain medical treatments
  • Financial concerns about medical bills and lack of insurance coverage
While these concerns are valid, it is important to remember that delaying or refusing medical treatment can cost you more in the long run, both in terms of your health and your legal claim. Why Am I So Tired After My Charleston Car Crash?

After a car crash, your body undergoes physical and emotional stress, which can lead to extreme fatigue. Injuries, even those that seem minor, can drain your energy as your body works to heal. Adrenaline and shock from the accident can mask pain initially, but once those effects wear off, exhaustion can set in. Additionally, anxiety, sleep disturbances and the stress from dealing with accident-related matters can contribute to feeling overly tired. Fatigue can also be linked to internal injuries that might not be immediately apparent, such as whiplash, concussions or soft tissue damage. These injuries can disrupt your normal sleep patterns and cause lingering pain, both of which are major contributors to post-accident exhaustion.

When Should I See a Doctor About Car Crash Fatigue?

You should see a doctor if your fatigue after a car crash lasts longer than a few days or if it is affecting your ability to function normally. Here are some signs that indicate it is time to seek medical attention:
  • Fatigue lasts more than a few days
  • You have trouble working or completing daily tasks
  • You experience headaches, dizziness or memory problems
  • Sleep disturbances or trouble resting

  • You notice new or increasing pain alongside fatigue

What Injuries Could Make Me Feel Unusually Tired?

Identifying these hidden injuries can help explain your exhaustion and guide you toward the right treatment.

Whiplash and Soft Tissue Injuries

Whiplash and other soft tissue injuries can cause pain and stiffness, leading to exhaustion as your body works to heal. Some other symptoms of whiplash and soft tissue injuries may include limited motion in the neck area and headaches.

Concussions or Mild Traumatic Brain Injury

Even a mild concussion can disrupt sleep patterns and cause fatigue, headaches and difficulty concentrating. After a concussion or any head injury, the brain requires more energy to heal. This demand for energy can result in physical and mental exhaustion. Additionally, a concussion, could cause sleep disturbance such as insomnia or excessive sleepiness.

Internal Injuries

Internal injuries, such as damage to organs or blood vessels, may not show symptoms right away but can lead to fatigue as your body responds to the trauma. For instance, blood loss from internal bleeding reduces oxygen circulation, leading to fatigue.

Spinal Injuries

Damage to the spine, including misalignments or nerve compression, can cause chronic pain and fatigue. Spinal injuries that affect nerve pathways can disrupt normal muscle functions and sensory signals, making daily activities more strenuous. The constant strain of compensating for spinal injuries can deplete a car crash victim’s energy, leading to poor sleep quality and persistent exhaustion.

How Long Could Fatigue Last After a Car Accident?

How long post-accident fatigue lasts varies from person to person, depending on the severity of your injuries and how your body is healing. For some people, fatigue may only last a few days or weeks as the body recovers from injuries and the traumatic experience of being in a car accident. However, if you sustained severe internal injuries, like whiplash or a concussion, you may also continue to feel tired. If you continue to feel fatigued for more than a couple of days, you should seek additional medical attention to rule out more serious injuries and/or get the treatment you need.

How Does Post-Accident Fatigue Affect Your Injury Claim?

Fatigue can also affect your ability to get through a work day or even do simple household tasks. Getting the treatment you need as soon as possible can make a difference not only in your ability to fully recover, but also in ensuring those damages are included in the overall value of your claim so you can be compensated fairly.

Impact on Work and Earning Capacity

Fatigue can make it difficult to return to work or perform job duties, which can affect your earning capacity and overall financial stability. You may not be able to complete certain tasks within a timely manner like you once did before the accident. This could mean that you may have to switch to a job in another industry, especially if you have permanent injuries.

Difficulty in Documenting Symptoms

Fatigue can also make it harder to track and document your symptoms, which is crucial for proving the extent of your injuries. For example, fatigue could mask injuries like sprains, fractures and concussions, causing victims to not detect symptoms for these injuries right away.

Medical Evidence

Consistent medical records showing how fatigue has impacted your life helps to strengthen your claim. However, if you have not sought treatment or have missed follow-up appointments, you may not have the evidence needed to prove that fatigue is linked to a car crash or that it exists. As a result, you may not get the full compensation that you need to recover from these injuries.

How Can Prescription Medication Affect My Driving?

Effects from prescription medication can cause drivers to swerve in and out of lanes or loose control of their vehicle. Even medications prescribed by trusted healthcare professionals can create dangerous driving conditions if not carefully managed. Prescription medications can significantly impair driving performance by:
  • Causing drowsiness or sedation
  • Reducing reaction times
  • Blurring vision
  • Causing dizziness
  • Impairing cognitive function
  • Decreasing motor coordination

What Types of Prescription Medication Could Lead to a Car Accident?

Several categories of prescription medications can compromise driving safety, such as:
  • Opioids: Used for managing pain and can cause drowsiness, slowed reaction times and impaired coordination.
  • Benzodiazepines: Medications like Xanax and Valium could be prescribed for anxiety and insomnia, which can lead to drowsiness, dizziness and poor judgment.
  • Antidepressants: Antidepressants like Prozac and Zoloft are used to treat depression but can lead to dizziness or blurred vision.
  • Antihistamines: This medication is used for allergies and cold symptoms. Drugs like Benadryl can cause drowsiness and reduced concentration.
  • Sleep Medications: Medication for individuals who have trouble sleeping can cause drivers to feel drowsy. For example, Ambien is a common sleep medication that is known for increasing the risk of accidents.

What Symptoms Could Lead to an Accident After Taking Prescription Medication?

Recognizing potential driving risks involves understanding specific symptoms:
  • Excessive yawning or feeling extremely tired
  • Difficulty maintaining lane position
  • Delayed reaction to traffic signals or sudden movements
  • Feeling disconnected or "foggy"
  • Feeling unusually relaxed or disoriented

Is It Illegal To Drive After Taking Prescription Medication?

In South Carolina, driving under the influence (DUI) laws still apply to prescription medications if they impair your ability to drive safely. While having a valid prescription is legal, driving while impaired is not. Under Section 56-5-2930, this law states that it is illegal to drive a vehicle under the influence of any substance, including prescription medication, if it impairs your ability to drive safely. Even with a valid prescription, you can be legally responsible if your medication causes a car accident. Law enforcement can still charge you with:
  • Driving under the influence
  • Reckless driving
  • Negligent operation of a vehicle

What Should I Do if I'm Injured Due to a Driver Being on Prescribed Medication?

Proving medication-related impairment requires thorough investigation and gathering evidence. If you have been injured in a car crash because another driver was impaired from prescribe medication, it is highly recommended to seek medical attention and reach out to a licensed car accident attorney. They can help you with filing a claim and navigating the complex legal process. If you have been involved in an accident potentially caused by prescription medication, take these steps:
  • Document everything at the accident scene
  • Get diagnostic tests for your injuries
  • Collect contact information from witnesses
  • Request a copy of the police report
  • Keep all medical records

How Can Drivers Prevent Driving Under the Influence of Prescription Medication?

Before drivers operate a vehicle, it is important that they know the preventative measures that they need to take to avoid any road hazards. Some steps that can be taken to prevent impaired driving due to prescription medications are:

Understanding Your Medication

Always read the label and warnings on your prescription medications. Look for any indications that the medication may cause drowsiness, dizziness or impair your ability to drive.

Consult Your Doctor

Ask your healthcare if your medication might affect your driving. They can provide you with guidance on when to take your medication and whether it is safe to drive while under certain medications.

Monitor Your Reaction

Everyone’s body react differently to medication. Pay attention to how you feel after taking your medication. If you experience any symptoms such as drowsiness or blurred vision, avoid driving.

Avoid Mixing Medication

Be cautious about taking multiple medications at once. Sometimes the combination of multiple medications could increase the risk of impairment. Also, avoid mixing medication with alcohol as it can cause you to become impaired before you drive.

Plan Ahead

If you know that you have to take medication that could impair your ability to drive, take alternative transportation like Uber, a public transit or ask a friend or family member for a ride.

Stay Informed

Stay up to date with any new information about your medications and their potential side effects. Your pharmacist can provide you with resourceful information.

What Permanent Injuries May Result From a Car Accident?

A permanent injury is one that does not heal completely, or a condition that will continue to affect you for the rest of your life. These types of injuries often lead to chronic pain, loss of function and in some cases, permanent disability. Some common examples of permanent injuries sustained in car accidents include:
  • Traumatic brain injuries affecting cognitive function
  • Spinal cord damage leading to paralysis
  • Severe burns causing disfigurement
  • Loss of limbs requiring prosthetics
  • Joint injuries resulting in chronic pain
  • Vision or hearing loss
  • Nerve damage causing persistent numbness
The impact of these injuries extends beyond just physical pain. Many people with permanent injuries face challenges related to employment, personal relationships and daily activities. Some may need lifelong medical care, assistive devices or ongoing therapy.

How Do I Calculate the Value of My Charleston Car Accident Claim?

While every car accident case is different, permanent injury settlements could range from hundreds of thousands or more. Factors impacting the overall value of your claim include:

Extent and Severity of Your Injuries

The more severe and permanent the injury, the higher the potential value of your claim. For example, an amputation or paralysis will typically result in a much larger settlement compared to a broken bone that heals within a few months. If your injuries cause permanent disability, requiring ongoing care or preventing you from working, the value of your claim will reflect these long-term consequences.

Medical Expenses

The cost of medical treatment after a car crash plays a significant role when determining the value of your claim. For permanent injuries, treatment costs can add up quickly and may include:
  • Emergency care immediately following the accident
  • Diagnostic testing
  • Surgery or other major medical procedures
  • Long-term physical therapy
  • Assistive devices (e.g., wheelchairs, prosthetics)
  • Pain management
  • Home healthcare services
  • Rehabilitation therapy
  • Pain and suffering
In South Carolina, victims can recover compensation for past, present and future medical expenses. If your injuries require lifelong medical treatment, this can significantly increase the value of your claim.

Lost Wages and Loss of Earning Capacity

If your permanent injuries prevent you from working or significantly limit the type of work you can perform, you are entitled to compensation for lost wages. This includes both the wages you have already lost and the wages you will lose in the future. The longer the impact of your injury on your ability to earn a living, the more compensation you may be able to claim for loss of earning capacity. If your injury limits your ability to work in the same field or results in a permanent reduction in income, the value of your claim will reflect this financial loss.

Pain and Suffering

Pain and suffering is a non-economic damage that compensates you for the physical pain, emotional distress and reduced quality of life caused by your injuries. Unlike medical expenses, pain and suffering damages do not have an exact formula. However, the more severe and permanent the injury, the higher the potential compensation. Some of the pain and suffering factors that may influence the value of your claim include:
  • The intensity and duration of pain
  • Whether you will experience ongoing pain for the rest of your life
  • The emotional toll of living with a permanent disability
  • The impact the injury has on your mental health (depression, anxiety, PTSD)
  • The way your injury affects your ability to participate in normal activities or enjoy life

Impact on Daily Life and Relationships

Permanent injuries often lead to changes in a person’s daily life, including a reduced ability to perform everyday tasks, like driving, cooking or caring for children. The ability to engage in social, recreational or family activities may be severely impacted. The more your injury alters your ability to live a normal, fulfilling life, the greater the value of your claim. Additionally, how your injury affects your relationships with your spouse, children or other close family members should be factored into your compensation.

Insurance Coverage and Liability

The amount of insurance coverage the at-fault driver carries affects the value of your claim as well. South Carolina law requires drivers to carry a minimum of $25,000 in liability insurance per person and $50,000 per accident for bodily injury. However, if the at-fault driver is underinsured or uninsured, this can complicate the claims process. If you have uninsured or underinsured motorist coverage, your own insurance policy may come into play. In some cases, these policies can help cover the costs of permanent injuries when the at-fault driver has insufficient coverage.

Dangerous Rural Highways in the Charleston Area

Charleston's rural areas have several dangerous routes where drivers need to be especially alert and take precautionary measures. These hazardous major rural routes include:
  • Highway 17 North: This highway runs through the towns of Awendaw and McClellanville. This remote route is known for its high traffic volume and wildlife crossings, which increases the risk of a crash.
  • Highway 61:This remote highway, also known as Ashley River Road, considered hazardous due to its narrow lanes and lack of shoulders.
  • Highway 41:  Another well-known rural highway that runs through Francis Marion National Forest. It dangerous to drivers, especially in low light and adverse weather conditions, due to limited lighting and sharp curves.
  • Highway 45: Drivers may be involved in a car accident on this highway due to its higher speeds, lack of safety features and limited emergency services.

Why Are Rural Roads So Dangerous?

Rural roads near Charleston present unique challenges that many drivers underestimate, such as:

Limited Emergency Response Available to Due Being Remote

After an accident, help takes longer to arrive in some rural areas. This can create critical and devastating circumstances for crash victims who are severely injured. For example, if someone suffers severe burns or lacerations, getting emergency medical care could make the difference in how well the victims recover.

Poor Road Maintenance

Rural roads are often maintained less frequently than city streets. Potholes, crumbling shoulders and faded lane markings add to already treacherous driving conditions. Poorly maintained roads during adverse weather make it even more challenging for drivers to see at night. For example, uneven lanes may cause side-swipe car crashes. Potholes in bad condition could cause a vehicle’s tire to blow out, making a driver lose control of their car.

Lack of Safety Features

Unlike urban roads, many rural routes lack the following safety features. These safety features are designed to help drivers avoid accidents and view hidden hazards.
  • Guardrails
  • Reflective markers
  • Adequate shoulder space
  • Streetlights
  • Clear signage

Environmental Factors

Common natural hazards in Charleston’s rural area include:
  • Flooding During Heavy Rain: If there is flooding in a particular area, vehicles may get stuck. Depending on how high the water rises, some drivers could drown in their vehicles.
  • Wildlife Crossings: Deer or wild boars could suddenly dart into the road. If drivers are unable to see them, it could cause a collision.
  • Fallen Trees and Branches: In rural areas, maintaining the roads can be difficult due to the exclusivity of the area. Speeding drivers risk crashing into large, fallen trees or branches.
  • Standing Water After Storms: Depending on the road, standing water could form after a storm, causing some vehicles to get stuck in mud. Standing water may also cause drivers to swerve, leading to a hydroplane crash.

Driver Behavior

Some drivers may be more reckless on rural roads, but these habits could lead to a car crash.
  • Higher speeds due to less traffic
  • Increased distracted driving
  • Overconfidence on familiar roads
  • Impaired driving due to fewer ride-share options

Are Fatal Car Accidents More Likely To Happen on Rural Roads?

According to the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration, rural accidents account for about 43 percent of all traffic fatalities from 2017 to 2021. These are the types of accidents that are likely to be fatal when driving in rural areas:
  • Head-On Collisions: If there are not enough traffic signs or lane markings, drivers may maneuver into the wrong lane, causing head-on collisions.
  • Single-Vehicle Accidents: Vehicles could be involved in a single-vehicle crash if the roads have sharp curves or lack guardrails.
  • Night-time Crashes: Night-time crashes are likely to happen if there are not enough streetlights, which could make it difficult to see other drivers.
  • Rollover Crashes: Rollover crashes are more likely to occur in rural areas when vehicles try to take sharp turns too quickly. SUVs, vans and  trucks, which have a higher center of gravity, are especially likely to flip over in this situation.

What Can Drivers Do To Prevent Car Crashes?

Drivers can significantly reduce their risk of crashing along a rural highway by following several key safety practices.

Slow Down

Reduce your speed and maintain extra following distance, especially at night or during bad weather.

Drive Defensively

Be prepare for unexpected curves and wildlife crossings. Keep your headlights on at night, especially if there are not enough streetlights.

Avoid Distractions

Avoid distractions like cell phones. Rural roads have fewer safety features and require more focused attention. In these areas, you could encounter farm equipment, wildlife or stopped school buses around blind curves.

Maintain Your Vehicle

Regular vehicle maintenance is crucial. Before traveling on rural routes, ensure your tires, brakes and lights are in good condition.

Watch Out for Shoulder Drop-Offs

Watch for shoulder drop-offs and avoid sudden steering corrections if your wheels drift off the pavement. Instead, slowly ease off the accelerator and gradually return to the road.

Keep Essential Items in Your Car

If you often drive in rural areas, having these items in your car could be helpful, as you may not have access to roadside assistance or emergency responders.
  • First aid kit
  • Flashlight
  • Reflective triangles or flares
  • Fire extinguishers
  • Spare tire, jack and lug wrench
  • Jumper cables
  • And more

Who Is Liable for a Rideshare Crash?

There are many contributing factors that impact who may be liable in rideshare crashes. To start with, it is important to determine what happened, which is why investigators carefully examine the crash scene and talk to the drivers involved. They will also get statements from any witnesses who saw the crash as it happened. Getting video coverage may be more likely when a rideshare driver is involved. Lyft and Uber drivers sometimes install a dashcam in their vehicles as further protection in the event they are involved in a crash. Depending on the outcome of the investigation and the story the evidence tells, multiple parties could be responsible. Below are some parties who may be fully or partially liable for damages resulting from a rideshare crash:
  • Rideshare Drivers: Uber, Lyft or other rideshare drivers could be liable if their negligence led to the crash that injured you.
  • Other Drivers: Other drivers who hit the Uber or Lyft car you were riding in may be responsible, or at least partially liable for the crash.
  • Vehicle Manufacturer: The manufacturer of a defective rideshare vehicle could be liable if the defect contributed to the crash.
  • Government Entities: Though less common, a local or state agency may be liable if poor road conditions results in a crash, especially if it is due to a lack of maintenance.
  • Rideshare Companies: Uber, Lyft and other rideshare companies might share liability in certain circumstances.

Who Pays for My Damages?

Any compensation you may be eligible for will typically come from the insurance policy of the party or parties deemed liable. In rare cases, it could come from some where else, such as a government entity or another third party. In a rideshare crash, you may be eligible to seek compensation for your medical costs and other damages from the following sources:

Rideshare Company Insurance

Both Uber and Lyft provide insurance coverage for their drivers. The coverage available, however, depends on the driver's status at the time of the accident:
  • If the app was off, the driver's personal insurance applies.
  • If the app was on but no ride had been accepted, the company provides limited liability coverage.
  • If a ride was accepted or a passenger was in the car, the company provides up to $1 million in coverage.

At-Fault Driver's Insurance

If another driver caused the crash, their insurance would be the primary source of compensation.

Your Own Insurance

Your personal auto insurance, might sometimes come into play as well. This is particularly true if the at-fault parties have insufficient coverage or no coverage. In a situation like that, your uninsured/underinsured motorist coverage would help to cover your damages. For instance, say an at-fault driver has some coverage, but it only covers 70 percent of your compensation. If eligible, then you may be able to cover the remaining 30 percent of your damages through your uninsured/underinsured motorist coverage.

Other Liable Parties

If a vehicle manufacturer or government entity is found liable, their insurance or funds would provide compensation.

What Type of Compensation May I Seek from a Rideshare Crash?

Every rideshare crash involves different scenarios, potentially requiring various compensation. In a high impact collision, rideshare passengers may have severe injuries that cause them to need compensation for surgery and other related medical bills. You may be entitled to several types of compensation such as:
  • Medical expenses: This covers emergency treatment, hospital stays, surgeries, medications and future medical care
  • Lost wages: If your injuries cause you to miss work, you can seek compensation for lost income, including future earnings if you're unable to return to your job.
  • Pain and suffering: This non-economic damage compensates for physical pain and emotional distress caused by the accident.
  • Property damage: If your personal property was damaged in the crash, you can seek compensation for repairs or replacement.
  • Loss of enjoyment of life: Compensate for injuries that prevent you from enjoying hobbies or activities, you once did before the crash
  • Punitive damages: Use to punish the wrongdoers in cases of extreme negligence or intentional misconduct

Risks of Driving With Loud Music

Drivers have a legal duty to stay focused on the road. Loud music can become distracting and disrupt a driver's ability to pay attention, which could lead to following types of distractions:

Cognitive Overload

Drivers may experience cognitive overload when the brain is overwhelmed by too many things happening at once. For instance, loud music with complex lyrics could leave drivers with less mental capacity to process important information. A driver could be too busy singing the lyrics to a song and fail to see a traffic light or stop sign, causing them to fail yield the right of way. This could in a crash if another vehicle is already traveling through the intersection.

Auditory Distraction

Auditory distractions are external sounds that prevent drivers from hearing vital cues on the road or highway. Loud music is an auditory distraction that conceals crucial environmental noise around you as you drive. For instance, it can conceal sirens, horns and tire screeches. If drivers cannot hear emergency vehicles approaching, it could lead to a serious crash involving another driver or emergency vehicle.

Attention Shifts

Loud music can cause drivers to shift their attention between listening to music and paying attention to the road. This shift can result in delayed responses to changes in traffic conditions or obstacles. For instance, if a driver is engaging in their music, they may not realize that they must slow down due to traffic congestions. As a result, drivers may not react swiftly to sudden changes, causing them to rear-end a vehicle in front of them.

The Impact of Loud Music in Charleston

Driving in Charleston is already tricky due to its historic cobblestone streets, busy tourist areas and community events. Loud music can present these driving challenges:

Narrow, Historic Streets

Charleston's historic district is beautiful, but has some narrow streets that limit visibility. Drivers must stay alert for other cars, pedestrians and cyclists. Loud music can muffle sirens and horns that distract drivers, making it harder to notice the signs of potential hazards and increasing accident risks.

Heavy Tourist Traffic

Tourist traffic in Charleston can create unpredictable driving conditions. Visitors may not be familiar with local road rules or the flow of traffic, particularly if they end up on one of the many one-way streets. Loud music can distract drivers from adapting to these unpredictable patterns, making it harder to navigate safely through busy downtown areas.

Pedestrian-Friendly Zones

Charleston is known for its vibrant pedestrian zones, including Broad Street and Rainbow Row. Pedestrian-heavy areas require extra vigilance. Drivers playing loud music might not notice pedestrians crossing streets or walking near the road, increasing the risk of pedestrian accidents.

How to Reduce Car Crash Related to Loud Music

Understanding the risks of loud music is the first step toward safer driving. Here are practical strategies to mitigate these risks:

Keep Volume at a Safe Level

One of the simplest ways to reduce the risks associated with loud music is to keep the volume at a moderate level. Ensure that the music does not overpower important sounds from the environment. The general recommendation is to keep the volume low enough so that you can hear sirens and other critical auditory cues.

Choose Music Wisely

The type of music you listen to can have an impact on your driving. Fast paced or highly energetic music can be more distracting than soothing or instrumental music. Opt for music that is calming and less likely to cause cognitive overload. Instrumental tracks or music with fewer lyrics may be less distracting and help you to maintain focus.

Avoid Distractions While Driving

Adjusting the music or making changes to the audio system while driving can be distracting. Minimize these interactions by setting up your playlist or radio stations before you start driving. If you need to adjust your any settings, pull over safely before doing so.

Be Mindful of Your Well-Being

Your own state of mind and physical condition play a role in how music affects your driving. If you are feeling tired or stressed, loud music can exacerbate these feelings and impair your driving further. Ensure that you are well-rested and in a good mental state before getting behind the wheel.

What Types of Eye Injuries Could Occur in a Car Crash?

Car crash eye injuries can occur in numerous ways. The airbag could hit you in the face or eyes when it deploys. If you are in the front seat, you could strike the dashboard or other hard surfaces inside the vehicle. Some people who sustain eye injuries may get hit by flying debris caused by the crash, such as shattered glass, pieces of metal or plastic, objects in the car or something else. In some cases, an airbag may deploy improperly, causing your eyes to be exposed to hazardous chemicals. Eye injuries that are commonly occur in a car wreck include:

Black Eye

Direct trauma to your eyes or the area around your eyes could cause your eyes to bleed, leading to tissue discoloration and a black eye. One way this could happen, for example, is if you hit the side of the door or steering wheel during the impact.. A black eye is not necessarily serious, but it is not easy to tell if other damage may have occurred, such as a torn retinae. In some cases, victims may develop "raccoon eyes" which simply means you have two black eyes.  This distinction is important, however, because it could be an indication of a brain injury.

Lacerations

Flying glass from a shattered window or windshield during a car crash could cut your eyelids. Serious eyelid lacerations can cause underlying damage to your eyeball, socket, retina or another part of the eye.

Orbital Fractures

It usually takes excessive force to break or fracture the bones in your eye socket. For example, if you hit your eye on the steering wheel due to the impact of a car crash. Orbital fractures are sometimes associated with serious brain or eye injuries that can affect coordination or even cognitive abilities.

Globe Ruptures

Blunt trauma or penetration of an eye can damage the cornea or sclera, the outermost layers of the eye. For example, the quick combustion of an airbag (less than a second) could mean a forceful impact on your face and, potentially, your eye.

Hyphema

When blood enters your eye’s anterior chamber, it becomes visible on your eyeball. A hyphema is typically caused by trauma to your eye and requires immediate medical attention to avoid permanent vision loss.

Chemical Burns

If your eye becomes exposed to any leaking chemicals from the vehicle after a car crash, you could suffer a chemical burn to your cornea or stem cells, leading to irritation or even blindness.

Traumatic Cataracts

Trauma to the eye could cloud your lens, causing blurred vision. Traumatic cataracts can gradually develop in the eye over time, so it is important to seek immediate medical attention if you experience any changes in your vision after a crash.

Retinal Detachment

The retina is the light-sensitive layer of tissue located in the back of your eye. A blow to your head during a car crash could rip the retina from the blood vessels in your eye. If you suffer from retinal detachment, your eyes may feel heavy, and you may see flashes or floaters. Retinal tears or a retinal detachment is an immediate emergency. Do not delay going to the ER as it could result in permanent vision loss.

Vitreous Hemorrhage

The vitreous humor is the gel between your retina and eye lens. Blunt trauma to your eye can cause hemorrhaging (bleeding) into the vitreous humor. Severe bleeding can be extremely dangerous if left untreated, potentially causing blindness.

Optic Nerve Damage

A blow to the eye during a car crash can put enough pressure on your optic nerve to bleed, cut off circulation and possibly cause permanent blindness.

Traumatic Brain Injuries (TBIs)

A TBI is caused by violent shock or impact to the head. This could result in different types of visual impairment, such as:
  • Blurry vision
  • Double vision
  • Loss of eye coordination
  • Light sensitivity
  • Visual memory loss

Symptoms of Eye Damage

If you suffered an eye injury from a car crash, you may experience some of the following symptoms:
  • Itchy eyes
  • Flashes of light
  • Swelling around your eye
  • Dark spots when you blink
  • Blood in or around your eyes
  • Blurry vision when you try to focus on an object
  • Reduced eye coordination or movement when you try to look up, down or peripherally

Treatment Option for a Car Crash Eye Injury

There are various options for treating an eye injury. The treatment you receive will depend on how serious your injury is:
  • Medication: A doctor might prescribe a drug to help clear an infection in your eye or manage pain and inflammation.
  • Eye patch: An eye patch can protect your eye while it heals after your injury.
  • Eye drops or ointments: If your eye is inflamed or dry, eye drops and ointments may lubricate it, reduce inflammation or prevent infection.
  • Rehabilitation: Prescription glasses, cryotherapy (therapy using cold temperatures), magnification devices, filters, etc. are types of rehabilitation designed to help victims regain visual function after a severe eye injury.
  • Surgery: Some injuries require surgery to repair damage to the eye, such as with a retinal tear, or to remove foreign objects.

What Is a Head-On Collision?

A head-on collision is a devastating accident that occurs when two vehicles traveling in opposite directions crash into each other front-to-front. These accidents often happen on two-lane roads or highways. In urban areas of Savannah, they can occur when a driver crosses the center line or enters a one-way street in the wrong direction. The force of impact in these collisions is particularly severe, leading to significant damage and catastrophic injuries.

What Are Some Common Causes of Head-On Collisions in Savannah?

Head-on collisions are almost always the result of driver negligence or errors, including:
  • Distracted driving: Using phones, eating, or other activities that take attention off the road.
  • Drowsy driving: Fatigued drivers may nod off and drift into oncoming lanes without realizing it.
  • Impaired driving: Driving under the influence of alcohol or drugs impairs judgment and slows reaction time. Drivers may lose control, engage in reckless driving behavior or be so drunk they cannot tell they are headed the wrong way.
  • Improper passing: Attempting to pass traffic on two-lane roads without adequate visibility.
  • Wrong-way driving: Entering highways or one-way streets in the wrong direction.
  • Poor road conditions: Lack of clear lane markings or signage, especially in bad weather.
  • Speeding: Excessive speed reduces reaction time and control.
  • Mechanical failures: Issues like tire blowouts or brake failures can cause drivers to lose vehicle control.
  • Swerving to avoid obstacles: Sudden moves to avoid animals or debris may lead to lane departures.
  • Medical emergencies: Drivers experiencing health issues may lose control of their vehicles.
Drivers owe a legal duty of care to prevent causing harm to others. This includes staying focused on the road and not engaging in reckless or negligent behaviors that could cause a head-on crash.

How Is Liability Determined for a Georgia Head-On Collision?

If you were injured in a head-on crash, you may wonder how liability is determined for a head-on collision. Like most crashes, there needs to be a thorough investigation. Seeking legal help sooner, than later can help, as your attorney can immediately get to work gathering evidence before it gets lost or destroyed. Evidence that may help determine who caused the crash that injured you include police reports and witness statements, of course. Police will also look for physical evidence at the crash scene, such as the extent and location of vehicle damage, to help determine how fast the vehicles were going at impact. Insurance companies, crash scene investigators and legal teams will examine factors such as:
  • Vehicle positions after the crash
  • Skid marks on the road
  • Damage patterns on the vehicles
  • Dash cam, surveillance or traffic camera footage, if available
An experienced attorney can help gather and interpret this evidence to establish liability.

Worried You Might Be Partially At Fault?

Even if you were partially to blame for your car accident In Georgia, you may still be eligible to seek some percentage of compensation for your damages.

Georgia Follows a Modified Comparative Negligence Rule

In Georgia, the concept of modified comparative negligence applies. For drivers involved in a crash, it means they can seek compensation for damages as long as they are less than 50 percent at fault. Drivers assessed with 51 percent of the fault – or higher – cannot recover any compensation. If you are assessed with a percentage of fault for your accident, any awarded compensation will be reduced by your degree of fault.

What Types of Injuries Are Caused by Head-On Collisions?

Head-on collisions often result in catastrophic injuries due to the combined force of two vehicles traveling in opposite directions. The sudden deceleration and impact can cause a wide range of traumatic injuries, affecting various parts of the body. Common injuries from head-on collisions include:
  • Traumatic brain injuries (TBI)
  • Spinal cord injuries
  • Whiplash and neck injuries
  • Chest trauma, including broken ribs and sternum
  • Internal organ damage
  • Fractures, especially to the legs, arms, and pelvis
  • Facial injuries and dental trauma
  • Lacerations and contusions
  • Psychological trauma, including PTSD
These injuries can have long-lasting effects on a victim's life. Prompt medical attention is essential, not only for health reasons but also for documenting injuries for legal purposes.

Get Medical Attention

Accepting medical attention at the scene could help protect your health from immediate harm. Track Medical Expenses

Keep all medical records and invoices, as this evidence becomes part of your overall claim. You should also be diligent to follow your doctor's advice as this may help to ensure a faster and more optimum recovery.

Be Careful What You Say

Never discuss fault at the crash scene, with the other driver, the insurance company or anyone except your attorney. Even if you think you are at fault, you should just stick to the facts. Crash scene investigators can determine fault. Never lie or exaggerate about what happened or about your injuries.

How Dangerous Is Distracted Driving in Savannah?

Distracted driving continues to be a leading cause of serious car crashes across the country. In Savannah, also, the city has seen a rise in distracted driving crashes due to individuals engaging in these and other behaviors behind the wheel:
  • Texting and driving
  • Taking videos or selfies

  • Tending to children in the backseat
  • Fiddling with GPS, music controls and other technology
  • Eating and/or drinking
